title: Chapter 63: Six Clockwork Men, Part 5 of 5: Four Notes
html:
She took Moll his supper herself.
Mrs. Oddie had it ready on the tray, the way she had his breakfast ready every morning: a bowl of mutton broth with a heel of bread in it, and a mug of small beer, and a spoon. Wren carried it up the dark stair with a candle on the edge of the tray, past the shut study door with the line of lamplight under it, past the white room, up to the top of the house. She knocked. Two, and then three. And went in.
Moll was sitting on the edge of his bed with his hands on his knees, exactly as he had been that morning. As if he had not moved all day. Perhaps he had not. The window was dark now, and there was rain on it. The small white room was very cold.
She put the tray on the chair. She put the candle on the washstand, where its light lay on his face and made deep shadows under his eyes and in the long lines of his cheeks.
Then she knelt in front of him, the way she did in the mornings, and took his hand, and turned it over.
She did not tap at once.
"Sergeant," she said. "I'm going away."
His face did not change. But she felt his hand go still under hers. Stiller than it had been.
"Tonight," she said. "North. With the Inquisitor's carts. I don't know for how long. A week. Two." She looked at the back of his old hand, at the brown spots on it and the thick blue veins. "Mrs. Oddie will bring your tray. She'll knock the right way. I've told her."
She had told her. She had stood in the kitchen and shown Mrs. Oddie the knock, on the table, two and then three, and Mrs. Oddie had watched without a word and then knocked it back, perfectly, on the scrubbed wood with her big knuckles.
"I don't know if she'll tap for you," said Wren. "The other thing. Heard. I'll show her. But I don't know if she'll—"
She stopped. She did not know why her voice was going like that.
She tapped it instead. On the back of his hand. Heard. The quick run, and the pause, and the slower run, and the one last tap.
His hand turned over under hers, the way it did. And his fingers tapped back. Heard.
And then, again, the other one. The new one from this morning. Long and short and long, and a pause, and a run of quick taps, and two slow ones, and the long one again. Exactly the same. Slower this time, and harder, as if he were pressing it into the skin of her hand so that it would stay.
Then stillness.
Wren looked up at him.
"I don't know what it means," she said. "I'm sorry. I don't know."
Moll looked at her.
And then, for the second time in four days, he did the thing he had done on Wednesday morning, the thing that had made her cry on the stair outside his door with the empty tray in her hands.
He hummed.
It was very quiet. A low, rough, cracked old man's hum, hardly more than a breath. But she knew it at once. She would have known it anywhere. Three notes. Up, and up, and up a little more.
Her three notes.
And then a fourth.
It went up again, a little, the fourth note, and then it stayed there. It hung. It did not come down. It hung in the cold air of the small white room the way a bird hangs in the wind over a cliff, very still, without any effort at all.
Then he stopped.
Wren knelt on the floor and could not move.
She had heard him hum it once before, on Wednesday. All four notes. She had cried. She had thought then that it was only because she was tired, and because the house was sad, and because an old man who never spoke had hummed her own tune back to her as if he knew it. She had thought that was why.
It was not why.
It was the fourth note. It was the way it went up, and hung. It was that she had been waiting for that fourth note her whole life, every time she hummed her three, without knowing she was waiting for it. And now she had heard it twice, and both times it had gone into her like a key into a lock that had been rusted shut for years, and turned, a little, and stuck.
"What comes after?" she whispered. "After that one? Sergeant. What comes after?"
Moll did not hum anymore.
He took his hand out of hers, gently, and put it back on his knee. He looked at the tray on the chair. Then he looked back at her, and his old tired hound's face did something she had never seen it do. The corner of his mouth moved. Only a little. Only for a moment.
Then he picked up his spoon.
Wren got up off the floor.
She stood by the door with her hand on the latch and watched him eat for a while, slowly, the bread soaking up the broth, the candle flame bending in the draft from the window. She thought about the three crates in the cart and the three in the other. About Ferrand's pale smile. About Rook's shaking hands, and the word through.
"I'll come back," she said. She did not know why she said it. She was not sure he could hear. "Sergeant. I'll come back. And I'll find somebody who knows the old calls. And I'll ask them what that one means." She drew a breath. "And then I'll come and tap it back to you. Properly. So you know I heard."
Moll did not look up from his broth. But his left hand, on his knee, moved. Two fingers lifted, and came down, and lifted, and came down.
Once. Then again.
She did not know that one either. But she thought, going down the dark stair with the candle, that she could guess.
Mrs. Oddie
Mrs. Oddie was sitting at the kitchen table when Wren came down with the empty tray.
She was not doing anything. That was what made Wren stop in the doorway. In two years Wren had never once seen Mrs. Oddie sit down. She was always at the range, or the sink, or the dresser, or the big flour bin in the corner, with her sleeves rolled up and her ham-like arms moving. Now she was sitting at the scrubbed table with her hands folded in front of her on the wood, and the lamp on the table beside her, and a pot of tea, and two cups.
Two cups.
"Sit," said Mrs. Oddie.
Wren had not known she had a voice. That was not quite true. She had heard her say yes, sir and no, sir to Kross, and mind the step to the coal man. But she had never heard her say anything to Wren that was not a nod.
She sat.
Mrs. Oddie poured the tea. It was very strong and very dark, the color of a peat stream, and she put milk in both cups without asking and pushed one across the table. Then she sat and looked at Wren over her own cup with small dark eyes set deep in her wide red face.
"North," she said.
"Yes, Mrs. Oddie."
"To the Glass."
Wren hesitated. Nobody had said that. Not in so many words. Not the Archon's card, not Kross, not Ferrand. North. The fens. Then the hills. Nobody had said the Glass.
"I think so," she said.
Mrs. Oddie nodded slowly, as if Wren had told her something she already knew.
She drank some of her tea. The range ticked as it cooled. Upstairs, very far off, the study clock struck the half hour.
"He went north once," said Mrs. Oddie. "Before your time. Before mine, nearly. My first winter in this house." She set her cup down. "Eighteen years back. Near enough. The winter of the fever."
Wren went still. "The fever?"
"In the north valleys. You'll not have heard of it. You'd have been a little thing." Mrs. Oddie turned her cup round on the table, slowly, by its handle. "Everybody was talking of it, that autumn. A fever in the valleys up past the fens. A whole village took with it. The Council voted money, and they sent men up to burn the houses so it wouldn't spread." She was quiet. "He went with them. He wasn't Inquisitor, then. He was young. Younger than you'd think. He went up with the men in gray in the first frost, and he was gone near a month."
Wren did not say anything. She did not drink her tea.
"I packed for him," said Mrs. Oddie. "Same as I packed for you. Stockings and grease and oatcake. I was new, and I didn't know what to put, and I put too much." Something moved at the corner of her mouth. "He brought half of it back. He said he'd not been hungry."
She looked at the lamp.
"He came back in the night," she said. "Near the end of the month. I heard the door. I came up from here with a candle to see, and he was sitting on the stair. On that step." She lifted her chin at the ceiling, at the hall above. "The fifth one. In his coat, with the snow still on it. Just sitting. I asked him did he want tea, and he said yes, and I brought it, and he didn't drink it." She was quiet for a long moment. "He sat there till morning. All night. Same as last night."
The kitchen was very quiet.
"He never said what he'd seen," said Mrs. Oddie. "Not to me. Not to anybody, I don't think. I never asked." She looked at Wren. "I never ask him anything. That's why I've lasted. You'll have noticed."
"Yes, Mrs. Oddie."
"But I'll tell you this, since you're going." Mrs. Oddie leaned forward a little over the table, and her voice dropped, though there was nobody to hear. "That step had no ring on it when I came to this house. It was new wood, pale as the rest. That ring's from him. From sitting there. Eighteen years of nights, on and off, when something's gone bad. You can see how many there've been."
Wren thought of the dark worn ring in the fifth step. The one she walked past every morning. She had thought it was from feet. From years of people walking up and down. She had never once thought it was from somebody sitting.
"Why are you telling me?" she said.
Mrs. Oddie sat back.
"Because he sat there last night," she said, "same as then. And then he picked you to go north with him." She picked up her cup. "And because somebody ought to know. In case."
"In case what?"
But Mrs. Oddie had said all she was going to say. She drank her tea, steadily, to the bottom of the cup, and set it down, and got up, and went back to the range, and rolled up her sleeves, and began to riddle the ashes out of the grate with a long iron poker, with her back to the room.
Wren sat at the table and drank her own tea, which had gone cold. She did not taste it.
The winter of the fever. In the north valleys.
She did not know why the words made her think of a beach below the Fish Stairs, and a gray stone with a white ring round it, and a small girl's hand closing on it in the wet shingle, a long time ago. She did not know why her hand had gone, again, to the empty pocket where the stone had been.
She took it away, and put her cold cup in the sink, and went upstairs to wait for midnight.
The Records Gate
She was at the Records gate at the half hour before midnight, as she had been told.
The yard was black. The rain had come on at dusk, a thin cold rain with sleet in it, and it was still falling, ticking on the cobbles and on the iron of the loading doors and on the brass hood of the Ash lamp over them. The lamp was the only light. Its hard blue-white glare lay on the wet black stones and made them shine like the skin of a fish, and everything outside its circle was darkness.
The carts were already there.
Two of them. Big closed carts, the kind the Ministry used for moving prisoners, black-painted, with high wooden sides and a curved canvas roof over hoops, and a small barred window high up at the front. Each was harnessed to a pair of heavy horses, gray in the lamplight, with their heads down in the rain and their breath smoking. A driver sat hunched on the box of each, in an oilskin cape, with the reins in his lap.
Behind the carts, four men on horseback. Enforcers, in the long gray coats of the Ministry, with short swords and carbines in leather buckets on their saddles. They sat their horses in a row, very still, the rain running off the brims of their hats. One of them nodded to Wren as she came into the light. She did not know him.
The tailboard of the first cart was down.
Wren went round to look, because she could not help it.
The crates were inside. Three of them, in the first cart, laid side by side on a bed of straw. The lids were down now, and roped. But through the boards, very faintly, under the ticking of the rain, she could hear the other ticking. Even. Steady. One clock, three times over.
They looked like coffins. Lying in straw in the back of a black cart in the rain at midnight, roped shut, they looked exactly like coffins being carried to a burying. She thought of the black cart at the bottom of Steeple Lane that morning, and the box with the black cloth over it, and looked away.
Ferrand was sitting on the bench at the front of the second cart, inside, under the canvas.
She saw him as she came round to it. The tailboard of that cart was down too, and inside, among the three roped crates, there was a narrow wooden bench against the front wall, under the small barred window, and Ferrand was sitting on it with his gray hat on his knee and his black notebook open on his hat. A shuttered lantern hung from a hook beside him, with just one shutter open, throwing a narrow slice of yellow light onto the page. He was writing.
He looked up and saw her.
"Cadet Halloway," he said, pleasantly. "How punctual. You'll ride with me, I think. It's drier." He moved along the bench, a little, to make room. "I'm afraid the company is rather quiet."
He smiled at the crates.
Wren did not smile back. She threw her canvas bag up into the cart, and climbed up after it over the tailboard, and sat down at the far end of the bench, as far from him as it allowed. The crates were very close. She could have reached out and touched the nearest one with her boot. She did not.
For a while neither of them said anything. The rain ticked on the canvas over their heads. The horses stamped and blew in the dark. Under the rain, under everything, the crates ticked too.
Then Ferrand said, without looking up from his notebook, "You keep a book, I believe, Cadet."
Wren went cold.
She did not move. She did not let her hand go to her breast pocket, where the small brown book lay buttoned in against her heart. She made her face do nothing at all, the way she had practiced in the cracked glass on the back of her door. She did not know whether it worked. Kross said her face did everything a face could do.
"Sir?" she said.
"Not sir. Ferrand." He turned a page. "A little book. Brown leather. Fourpence, on Quill Row, I should think. One sees them in the windows." He wrote something. "I keep one too, you see. We have that in common." He lifted his own black notebook a little, and smiled at it. "Mine is for His Excellency, of course. Everything in it is for His Excellency. Whose is yours for?"
Wren said nothing.
She thought of the pages. Woman, Coal Street, debt: the smell of her mother's hair. Boy, about seven, Fish Stairs, Health cart: his first fish. Line after line after line, in her small neat hand, of everything she had ever taken.
She thought: he cannot know what is in it. He cannot. Nobody has ever seen it. Nobody.
She thought: he knows it exists. He knows where it is. He knows what it cost.
"It's mine," she said. "Just mine."
"How nice," said Ferrand. "How very nice, to have something that is just one's own." He wrote. "I don't think I have ever had anything that was just mine. I don't think I would know what to do with it."
He did not say anything else about the book. He did not need to.
After a while he said, still writing, "You admire him, I think. The Inquisitor."
Wren looked at the crates.
"He's my master," she said.
"That isn't what I asked." Ferrand's pencil moved. "But it's a very good answer. It's the answer I would have given, in your place." He paused. "He's a very good man, you know. Inquisitor Kross. A very good, very careful, very tired man."
"Yes," said Wren, before she could stop herself.
"Yes." Ferrand looked up at her for the first time, in the narrow slice of yellow light from the lantern. His pale eyes were perfectly calm. "That is what worries His Excellency."
Wren could not think of anything to say to that. Anything at all. She sat on the bench with her hands in her lap and her heart beating very hard and slow, and the rain ticked on the canvas.
"His Excellency," said Ferrand, "is the kindest man I have ever known."
He said it very simply, the way you might say it is raining. He did not smile when he said it. For the first time since the vault, his face was not smiling at all. It was quite plain, and quite still, and his pale eyes had gone somewhere else, a long way off, the way eyes go when somebody is thinking of a person they love.
"People do not understand him," he said. "They think he takes things. He doesn't. Not really. He only takes away what hurts." He was quiet for a moment. "I had a great deal that hurt, once. When I was a boy. I don't remember any of it now. He took it all. Every bit. And I have never once, since, been unhappy." He looked down at his notebook again. "Not once. Can you say that, Cadet? Can anyone?"
Wren did not answer.
She was thinking of Moll's face, in the candlelight, when he hummed the fourth note. Of the way it had hung in the air. Of the way it had gone into her like a key.
She was thinking that she would not trade that for anything. Not for never being unhappy. Not for anything at all.
She did not say so.
Ferrand did not seem to expect her to. He wrote another line in his square, separate letters, and turned another page, and the shutter of the lantern creaked a little as the cart shifted on its springs.
She heard footsteps on the cobbles.
Kross came into the lamplight.
He was wearing a long black riding cloak, wet through, and his hat, and he was carrying nothing. He walked along the line of carts and horses without hurrying, looking at each one, the way he had looked at the crates in the vault. He spoke to each of the Enforcers in turn, low, a few words. She could not hear what. Each of them touched his hat. Then he came round to the back of the second cart and stood in the rain at the tailboard, looking in.
He looked at the crates. He looked at Ferrand. He looked, last, at Wren.
She waited for him to climb in.
He did not.
"I have a funeral on Sunday," he said. To Ferrand. Quietly, so that the drivers would not hear. "I'll catch you up at Thistle Ford."
Ferrand inclined his head. "Of course, Inquisitor."
"The north road to the toll. The dyke road to the fens. Then the drove road over the hills. You'll not lose it. It has walls." Kross paused. "You'll not wake them on the road. Not until you need them. Not for any reason."
"I would not dream of it."
Kross looked at him a moment longer. Then he looked at Wren again, and she thought for a moment he was going to say something to her. His mouth moved. But whatever it was, he did not say it.
He put up the tailboard himself, with his gloved hands, and slid the bolts home.
Then his voice came from outside, in the rain, to the drivers: "Go on."
The carts moved.
Wren felt it in the bench under her, a jolt and a lurch and then a heavy rolling sway, and heard the wheels grind on the wet cobbles, and the horses' hooves, and the creak of the harness. Through the barred window above her head she saw the blue glare of the Ash lamp swing past, and the black gateway of the Records yard, and then the lamp was behind them and there was only the dark, and the rain on the canvas, and the slow grind of the wheels on the street.
She twisted round on the bench and looked back through the small window at the back of the canvas.
Kross was standing alone in the middle of the empty yard in the rain, under the Ash lamp, in his black cloak, watching them go. He did not lift his hand. He only stood there, getting smaller, a thin dark figure in a circle of hard blue light, until the cart turned the corner into Mercer Street and he was gone.
Wren turned back and sat still.
The city went past outside the small barred window above her head, in pieces.
A gas lamp, yellow, on a corner, with rain slanting through its light. A shuttered shop. A tavern door, open, with red light and noise spilling out of it onto the wet street, and a man being sick in the gutter beside it, and then that was gone. A long blank wall. A bridge: she felt the cart tip up and then down again, and heard the hollow change in the sound of the wheels, and below it, very faint, the river. Another lamp. Another wall. Then the lamps got further apart, and then there were no more lamps, only the dark and the rain, and the houses on either side of the road were low and dark and few.
At the north gate the cart stopped.
She heard voices outside. A watchman's voice, rough and sleepy, asking who went there at this hour. One of the Enforcers' voices answering, short and flat. A pause. The watchman's lantern swung up to the barred window at the front of the cart, and for a moment a red face with a gray mustache peered in through the bars, and saw her, and saw Ferrand, and saw the crates, and went very still.
Ferrand looked up from his notebook and smiled at the face.
The face went away very quickly.
The gate creaked. The cart rolled on.
After the gate, the road changed under the wheels. It was not cobbles anymore. It was earth and stones, rutted and soft with the rain, and the cart lurched and swayed and jolted, and the crates shifted a little in their straw, and the ticking inside them did not change at all. Wren held on to the edge of the bench. Ferrand did not seem to notice the jolting. He sat as easily as if he were in a chair in a warm room, writing.
She looked down at her own hand, in her lap.
The back of it, where Moll had tapped. Twice today. The new pattern, the one she did not know. Long and short and long, and a pause, and the quick run, and the two slow ones, and the long one again. She could still feel it, she thought. Or she was imagining it. A faint warmth in the skin, where his old dry fingers had pressed it in so hard.
She closed her other hand over it, and held it there, and did not let go.
Outside, the rain came on harder. The road went north. Out into the dark beyond the city, toward the dyke road and the fens and the hills, and whatever lay beyond the hills that nobody would say the name of.
Ferrand had closed his lantern's shutter, all but a crack, and gone back to his notebook. She heard his silver pencil moving in the dark. She heard the rain. She heard the horses, and the wheels, and the creak of the cart. Out past the edge of the city, past the last of the gas lamps, past the north gate, onto the north road, toward the fens.
And under all of it, in the dark of the cart beside her, close enough to touch, she heard the ticking. Three crates in this cart. Three in the other. Six iron hearts, ticking together, slow and patient and even, on and on and on.
It sounded, she thought, like a roomful of clocks, waiting for the same hour.
